Austin publishes every road closure in the city and never publishes a single detour. This is what its open feeds actually said at the moment of this snapshot — including how much of it can be trusted.

Central Austin

Every full street closure, shaded by how much we believe it

Streets are drawn from the city's own centreline layer rather than map tiles. Solid lines are closures we can stand behind; dashed lines are permits whose own dates or notes suggest the work is finished. Rings mark clustered signal failures.

The hard part

Most of this feed cannot be trusted, and the city says so

Of 3,853 work zone records, the city has verified an end date on a handful and a position on none at all. Dates are permit windows, not work windows. Every record is scored, and only the top tier is ever allowed to send a notification.

Signal events

What the desk editor made of today

Clustering is arithmetic — distance and time decide that several signals are one event. Interpreting the cause is not, because each hypothesis is tested by a different lookup: digging permits beside the cabinets, a venue next door, a crash on the dispatch feed.

Data defect

The overnight sweep


    
Those records carry the moment a batch last counted them, not the
      moment the fault began. Clustering on them chains half the city into one meaningless event,
      and any duration derived from them is wrong — a signal unreachable for years reads as
      unreachable for hours. They are excluded, and items built on a swept timestamp say the onset
      is unknown rather than quoting a false figure.
